issues.legal_issue: The Chief Controlling Revenue Authority may interfere with a Collector’s order when that order is erroneous.
material_facts: The appellants challenged the Collector’s order before the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority under Section 56 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.
The Authority set the Collector’s order aside, in part on the ground that the Collector lacked jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court held that the Authority had power to interfere if the Collector’s order was erroneous, but found no defect in the Collector’s direction to take steps to realise stamp duty.
issues.conclusion: The Chief Controlling Revenue Authority had power to interfere with an erroneous Collector’s order, but the Collector’s direction in this case was not defective.
issues.legal_principle: Section 56 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, empowered the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority to interfere with the Collector’s order if it was erroneous. Under Janardan Reddy v. State of Hyderabad, a decision made without jurisdiction may be challenged through the same route as a decision made with jurisdiction.

predicates.revenue_revision_of_collector_order: A revenue authority is asked to review an order made by a Collector.
predicates.collector_order_erroneous: The Collector’s order contains an error.

issues.definition: When a revenue authority reviews a Collector’s order and the order contains an error, the authority may interfere with it.

issues.legal_issue: Delay does not bar further stamp-duty recovery steps that implement an earlier court direction to impound an instrument and send it to the Collector.
material_facts: The civil court directed that the award be impounded and sent to the Collector for necessary action.
The further steps were not taken promptly, and a party later applied to the Collector to have them taken.
The Collector’s orders were treated as follow-up steps implementing the civil court’s direction.
issues.conclusion: The Collector’s follow-up orders were not barred by limitation, and the Collector had to proceed with realisation of the escaped duty.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 33(5) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, limits action taken by the Collector on the Collector’s own initiative under Section 33(4). It did not bar delayed follow-up steps implementing the civil court’s direction to impound and transmit the instrument. The source of the reminder for those steps did not prevent their being taken.

predicates.stamp_duty_recovery_proceeding: The proceeding concerns recovery of escaped stamp duty on an instrument.
predicates.prior_court_direction_to_impound: A court directed that the instrument be impounded and sent to the Collector for necessary action.
predicates.delayed_steps_implement_that_direction: The Collector’s later steps implement the court’s direction rather than initiate a new action independently.

issues.definition: In a stamp-duty recovery proceeding, delay does not bar later steps that implement a court’s earlier direction to impound and transmit the instrument.

issues.legal_issue: The Collector may examine an instrument’s valuation when the applicable law expressly authorizes that examination.
material_facts: The proceeding concerned an award relating to property whose valuation was disputed.
The proceeding arose in a jurisdiction where an express statutory provision authorized the Collector to examine the correctness of valuation.
issues.conclusion: The Collector had power to inquire into the valuation of the property that was the subject matter of the award.
issues.legal_principle: Section 47-A, inserted by a Uttar Pradesh amendment to the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, expressly authorized the Collector to examine the correctness of valuation. Himalaya House Co. Ltd. v. Chief Controlling Revenue Authority did not prevent that inquiry where the applicable law contained this express authorization.

predicates.stamp_proceeding_involves_instrument_val: A stamp-duty proceeding concerns the valuation of property covered by an instrument.
predicates.applicable_law_authorizes_valuation_inqu: The law governing the proceeding expressly authorizes the Collector to examine the correctness of the valuation.

issues.definition: When a stamp-duty proceeding involves an instrument’s valuation and the governing law expressly authorizes valuation review, the Collector may inquire into that valuation.

issues.legal_issue: A proceeding limited to recovering stamp duty does not alter an earlier adjudication rejecting an award as a rule of court.
material_facts: An earlier adjudication rejected the request to make the award a rule of court, and subsequent applications for further review were dismissed.
The present proceeding concerned realisation of stamp duty on the award.
The Court confined its decision to the stamp-duty proceeding and clarified that the earlier adjudication’s effect had not disappeared or been modified.
issues.conclusion: The present judgment did not modify the earlier adjudication concerning the request to make the award a rule of court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court confined its decision to the limited scope of the stamp-duty recovery proceeding and expressly preserved the effect of the earlier adjudication and the orders dismissing further review.

predicates.stamp_duty_recovery_proceeding: The current proceeding concerns recovery of stamp duty rather than whether the award should be made a rule of court.
predicates.prior_adjudication_rejected_court_rule_r: An earlier adjudication rejected a request to make the award a rule of court.
predicates.further_review_was_dismissed: Applications seeking further review of the earlier adjudication were dismissed.

issues.definition: When a stamp-duty recovery proceeding follows an adjudication rejecting a request to make an award a rule of court and further review was dismissed, the recovery judgment does not modify that adjudication.
